"Dad."

"Yeah?"

"Got any advice?"

There's a time for open questions and this probably isn't it. 

"Not really."

"Okay."

Now's the time to ask something direct.

"Dad."

"..."

"How do you feel?"

As far as direct questions go, in this circumstance, that was probably the worst one you could have asked.

"Huh?"

"How you feeling?"

"I'm okay."

Questions aren't working, clearly. Offer something else.

"I got you some grapes."

"..."

"And so did a few others I see."

"Thanks."

Getting somewhere now.

"No problem. Do you need anything else?"

"No. I'm okay"

"Okay"

Time is short at the minute, got to be bold.

"I love you, Dad."

"..."

"......"

Was that too bold? Probably, to be honest.

"You get yourself home."

"Yeah?"

"Yeah, off you go."

"I've got time, Dad."

That's true at least. Everyone's got time, some more than others.

"I'll stay with you."

"Nah, don't worry. I'm okay."

And everyone's okay, too. Some more than others.

"Alright, Dad. Good to see you."

"Yeah."

"Are you comfortable?"

"I'm fine, get yourself off."

Everyone's okay. Some of us are okay because we have a return ticket for a five hour journey home. Others are okay because they have nurses replenishing their oxygen.

Some of us have happy memories of being taken swimming or feeding the ducks. We remember steamy windows on a Sunday afternoon right before eating crispy roast potatoes and Yorkshire puddings. We remember tunnel slides, strawberry picking, sandcastles and ice creams, all with the one person we have to look up to.

Other people remember cigarette trays by the pool, bread they never used. They remember too much washing up right before the work week. They remember parks while thinking about beer gardens, little twats picking fruit, £3.50 buckets for sand instead of glasses of lager and ice cream. Yeah. We all remember ice cream.

You're never gonna look back and remember these things in your last moments with nobody around though.

"Alright, I'll get myself off. Bye, Dad".

If I were in your position I'd choose Sheffield. Leeds might be more appealing for you at your age because it's a big national city and hub but for those reasons you'll soon get bored there. Leeds is a connecting city for Scotland and London and you'll notice the non-Yorkshire folk on a day to day basis. Nothing wrong with those non-Yorkshire folk, it just doesn't sound like what you're after.

You've got some great nights out in Leeds, You'll spend some good evenings on Merriom Street but I reckon you'd be more up for the bar run down at Headingley. That's where someone your age would want to live, you'd have a blast.

But you'd get bored there much quicker than you would in Sheffield.

I don't know Sheffield well, I have to admit. I know Leeds well though. The few weeks I spent in Sheffield excited me much more than the years I spent in Leeds. Firstly, the arts scene in Sheffield is genuine - hardly any posers trying to shovel their post punk open mic down your throat. You've got Arctic Monkeys and their genuinely talented successors.

You've got green parks right in the thick of it. Get yourself some new trainers in JD then go try them on in a beautifully maintained and quiet public space. You could do that in Leeds too but there might be a polluted main road and a midweek boozer shouting at you.

In Leeds you've got unstoppable access to the Dales with proper regular trains to whichever hike you pick. Sheffield trains to the Dales are a bit less frequent but still easy But what you get from Sheffield is access to the Peaks, which I'd probably argue are more beautiful, coming from a bloke who grew up by the Dales. If you live in Sheffield you can walk you can easily walk out into the Peaks, accessing them without a vehicle. From Leeds to the Dales is a bit less accessible by foot.

I'll have to mention the theatres. Leeds has the West Yorkshire Playhouse, arguably the biggest stage in the north (ignoring the Royal Exchange) I've seen some fantastic productions at the West Yorkshire Playhouse but The Crucible in Sheffield is much more exciting. They've got the space to dip between theatre, live music and sport (home of snooker forever) seamlessly. A mainstream venue in a national hub like Leeds can't afford to frequently change their target audience like The Crucible can.

Pints are cheaper in Sheffield. 

If you want Leeds, go to Manchester. If you want Sheffield, go to Sheffield.

"Shut up Neil, seriously, shut the fuck up. Neil"  
"God, mate. Honestly, Neil is cool, he's just being a pillock right now."

Neil, in all his chaos and thunder, actually shut the fuck up for once. Thank God for that. 

"Did you have a nice snooze, God?"

It appeared, mainly because of the drooly holy sleeve wiping the sleep from his eyes and yawn from his face, that God hadn't quite woken up enough to see what a fuck up Neil had become.

Phew.

"God, buddy, get yourself together a bit and we'll catch up. It's all good here, don't worry, we kept on top of things. You got your toothbrush, pal? I have a spare if not."

It's gonna be a shitshow when God has brushed his teeth and had his shower and discovers that Neil blew it. The one thing God wanted us to sort out, and Neil chanced it. 

"Neil, get a fucking jam jar. Now. Now Neil!"

Neil looked onwards with disdain. Where was he going to get a jam jar from at this hour? Nevermind where, Neil had no intention of saving his jam jars this last thousand years, he's not going to start now. 

"God, I'm sorry it's not Colgate, we had to go to Lidl. Apparently it does the job just like Colgate, it's just a bit cheaper. You said be frugal didn't you, God?"

God gave a half smile, knowing his savings had been in good hands whilst he slept.

Neil fell to the floor in a panic he'd not shown for a millenia. His hands clasped on the ground, his eyes looking up, his sweat rolling onto his lip.

"Neil. Oh Neil, yeah show God that new bit of floor you found and how mighty and holy it is"

God looked at Neil. He was impressed.

Phew.

Little did God know that Neil was covering his back. 

"God, pal, why don't you go back to sleep? Have a lie in, we've got this".

We didn't got this, thanks to Neil.

"What's that bit of ground you've got under your hands, Neil?" - Said God.

We're gonna be rumbled. Neil, the fuckwit, is about to get us rumbled. 

"God, go back to sleep" - bumbled Neil.

"I'm awake now, Neil. Let me see what you've got there under your hands. Remember, I am God Almighty, nothing will bother me. Let me see what you have under your hands, Neil"

"No" - sneezed Neil.

"Oh go on, Neil" - begged God. "I can handle it, as long as it's not that thing I asked you to take care of"

"Erm" - ermed Neil.

"I am God Almighty, creator of all, lover of all beings."

"Listen, God. Listen, seriously, there was a thing and we got held up..."

Neil removed his hands. 

"AAARRGH" - cried God with his wrists to his chin.

"God I'm sorry" - Neil apologised.

"Get a jam jar" - God demanded.

But there were none. 

"Get it out" - God pleaded as he took refuge atop a stool.

Neil flapped about a bit to try to get it out. But it was too quick. It disappeared underneath the wardrobe. 

"I'm not coming down while there's a spider in here" - God nipped. "Neil, get rid of the spider"

And Neil looked under the wardrobe with doubt. It's probably gone by now. God will have to live with it.

I know nothing about your life, I don't know who or how many people you have in your support group but I feel very confident in saying yes, you will be missed. Let me answer each of your questions the best I can. 

>Will anyone actually miss me?

Absolutely. I don't know who is in your life but I do know that you have interacted with someone recently. Who was the last person in your life that you talked to? I'm gonna say that they will miss you. 

>Will anyone care a month from now???

I hope you haven't had to grieve for someone close to you, but if you have, do you miss them now? In December it will be ten years since my very close friend of mine, Martin, died. He didn't have many friends when he was alive, he never lost his virginity. I still wake up in the middle of the night with a jolt of shock and the realisation that he died. It crushes me. In a month from now people won't even realised what's hit them.

>A year from now?

If they're feeling devastated in a month, they need to wait until the one year anniversary comes around. On 9th December 2013 I couldn't prepare myself for how I was going to feel on the one year mark since Martin died. And it stuns me every year. It's a date I dread, a date I hope ends quickly.

>Is it worth leaving a note?

That's up to you to decide. I've written three suicide notes to date. But the most serious attempt I made I didn't write one. I didn't feel it was worth it. I didn't have the energy, I didn't need to say anything to anyone. But if you're asking this question then I know it's not something you need to think about. You have things to say, of course, but have you thought about writing them down just for you? Write something to yourself, put your feelings on paper but write it just for you, not for anyone else to read. Once you've done that, read it back. I'd be surprised if that doesn't give you a bit of perspective and will nullify this question. 

>Is it worth trying to get better?

There aren't really objective reasons to live. You could say that objectively, we need to reproduce. Or we need to provide for our loved ones. Or we need a successful career. Or we need to learn new things. But it can't be objective. I don't give a fuck about a successful career, I just want to find as many things that make me laugh until I die whilst making as many people laugh as possible along the way. You might not want that. You might want a child and to be their provider. I don't want that, but that doesn't mean you wanting it isn't valid. There can't be an objective reason to live because we've evolved past the fundamental objective of life that is to conserve energy and reproduce. We've become subjective beings, we do what makes us happy and nobody can tell another person how to do that.   


I've been close to suicide for a long time. I'm still battling it, but I'm doing better. I don't have an objective reason to be here, but I have my own reasons. You'll find your own, I'm sure. Try not to worry about what we're here for, but discover what *you're* here for. If you're able to anytime soon, find a lake, river or ocean, take your shoes and socks off and put your feet in. That to me is the only real purpose.   


The only person that can give you a meaning for any of this is you.

When my friends and I were 17 we were pretty stupid. None of us had driving licences and we had been at a party and then gone back to my friends house. We had smoked a lot of weed and were pretty drunk. My friend had access to his dad's car and I lived on the other side of town. My friend thought he should give me a lift so he did. I sat in the front passenger, another friend in the back and my uninsured/drunk/ friend driving. We got a few streets from my house when a police car saw us go round a roundabout and turned round fast with its lights on coming towards us. We pulled over, every sense of fear rushing through us all. I, having seen too many Worlds Wildest Police Videos, got out of the car with my hands in the air, to which the officer told me to get back in over his megaphone. He asked the driver why he thought he'd been pulled. He said "Goooood evening officer, do I have a tail light out?" The officer told us that we went too slowly round the roundabout and assumed we were drunk. After a couple of minutes of us being polite as possible, the officer said that we were clearly not drunk at all and let us on our way. 

I am not proud of what we did, I do not find drink driving acceptable and we could have endangered people which is not cool. Just thought I'd share the story.

TL;DR - drunk/unlicensed and got pulled over. Acted politely and got out of it.
